newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore August export growth seen slipping.
newsitem.headline: Singapore August export growth seen slipping.

text.p: Singapore's export growth, which rose unexpectedly in July, is likely to slip back into negative territory in August as a global downturn in the electronics industry persists, economists said on Wednesday.
Eight financial institutions predicted on average in a Reuters poll that August non-oil domestic exports would fall by 0.8 percent in nominal terms on a year-on-year basis.
Forecasts ranged widely from a drop of 4.5 percent to a rise of 3.5 percent in the poll conducted on September 17.
This compares with a 6.4 percent rise in July and a 6.1 percent fall in June. Throughout last year and in the first half of 1996, growth often reached double digits.

"Electronics exports are going to drag the figures down again. Last month's bounce is not particularly sustainable over the medium term," said Desmond Supple, Southeast Asia economist at research firm I.D.E.A.
Electronics and related products accounted for almost half of Singapore's total industrial output and 60 percent of its non-oil exports in 1995.
Economists also varied in their predictions of when the electronics industry, hit by a slowdown in high technology markets in the United States, might see a turnaround.
Eddie Lee, regional economist at Vickers Ballas, was among the optimists.
"We are expecting the Christmas sales to boost demand and also the fall in prices" of electronics products to boost demand in the fourth quarter, Lee said.
Tay May Yuen, economist at Crosby Securities, agreed Christmas demand for personal computers and disc drives, coupled with increased production, would boost exports in the fourth quarter.
But Ng Bok Eng, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said Singapore's export growth would, at best, make a modest recovery by the first quarter of 1997.
"One of the reasons exports went up so significantly in July was the low base in the same period last year. That low base scenario will not happen again in August," he said.
Ng said the export slowdown would have a knock-on effect on other sectors of the economy, including financial services and transportation.
At the other end of the spectrum, Daniel Lian, regional economist at NatWest Markets, said August non-oil exports were likely to rise 3.5 percent.
"I'm expecting much slower growth compared to last year, but I really doubt we would dip into negative territory ... External demand hasn't really slowed down that much," Lian said.

But he said that if sagging exports in Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand had severely dented demand for Singapore's products and services, it would result in a "broad-based slowdown" for the island-nation.
